--- title: "Discriminative and generative models" description: "A discriminative model learns only the line between outcomes; a generative model learns the data well enough to invent new examples. Both answer the same presence question on the coastal survey, and agree where the data are dense." order: 5 categories: [foundations, supervised, classification] --- ## Two things a model can learn [Types of learning](types-of-learning.qmd) sorted methods by the data you hold. This page sorts them a second way: by the thing the model learns. Suppose the question is whether a species is present, given the water temperature. A model can learn one of two things. A **discriminative model** learns the answer directly: the chance that the species is present at each temperature. It draws the boundary between "present" and "absent" and nothing else. Most models in this course are discriminative, including linear and logistic regression. A **generative model** learns the data themselves. It describes the temperatures where the species was found, and separately the temperatures where it was not. To classify a new case, it asks which of the two descriptions fits that temperature better. Because it has learned the data, it can also *generate* new ones: plausible temperatures for a place where the species occurs. The tools that write text or draw pictures are generative models of the same kind, on a vastly larger scale. ::: {.diagram} ![The same data seen by two kinds of model. A discriminative model learns only the boundary between the groups; a generative model learns a description of each group, from which it can draw new examples.](img/discriminative-generative.svg){fig-alt="Two panels showing the same scatter of stations by temperature and depth: blue dots where the species was found, orange triangles where it was not. In the left panel, labelled discriminative, a dashed line separates the two groups. In the right panel, labelled generative, a shaded oval surrounds each group, and a hollow dot inside the blue oval is marked as a new example."} ::: ## Both kinds on the coastal survey ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: Both models below answer the presence question for the survey used in [Types of learning](types-of-learning.qmd), with temperature as the only input. They are fitted to the same three quarters of the stations and asked about the same three new stations, at 12, 9 and 5 °C. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75, strata = present) train <- training(split) new_stations <- tibble( station = c("shallow", "mid-depth", "deep"), temperature_c = c(12, 9, 5) ) ``` ::: ### A discriminative model: logistic regression Logistic regression, with a squared temperature term so the chance of presence can rise and then fall, is the discriminative model: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} discriminative <- logistic_reg() |> fit(present ~ temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2), data = train) bind_cols(new_stations, predict(discriminative, new_stations, type = "prob")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | temperature_c| .pred_yes| .pred_no| |:---------|-------------:|---------:|---------:| |shallow | 12| 0.8192281| 0.1807719| |mid-depth | 9| 0.8928872| 0.1071128| |deep | 5| 0.5837688| 0.4162312|
::: ::: For each new station it returns one thing: the chance of presence, and its complement. The species is likely at 9 °C and at 12 °C, and closer to a coin toss at 5 °C. That is all the model knows. ### A generative model: one bell curve per group The generative model describes the temperatures at stations with the species by a bell curve (a *Normal distribution*) with its own mean and spread, does the same for stations without the species, and records how common each group is. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} generative <- train |> group_by(present) |> summarise(mean = mean(temperature_c), sd = sd(temperature_c), share = n() / nrow(train)) generative |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|present | mean| sd| share| |:-------|----:|----:|-----:| |yes | 8.95| 2.39| 0.78| |no | 8.11| 3.71| 0.22|
::: ::: The two groups have similar mean temperatures, but the stations without the species spread much more widely: the species is missing mainly from the coldest and the warmest water. To classify a new station, **Bayes' rule** weighs the two descriptions: how well each bell curve fits the station's temperature, times how common that group is. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_present_generative <- function(temperature) { yes <- filter(generative, present == "yes") no <- filter(generative, present == "no") fit_yes <- yes$share * dnorm(temperature, yes$mean, yes$sd) fit_no <- no$share * dnorm(temperature, no$mean, no$sd) fit_yes / (fit_yes + fit_no) } new_stations |> mutate(.pred_yes = p_present_generative(temperature_c)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | temperature_c| .pred_yes| |:---------|-------------:|---------:| |shallow | 12| 0.8035139| |mid-depth | 9| 0.8461345| |deep | 5| 0.6606586|
::: ::: Because it holds a description of the data, it can also generate new data. Here are five plausible temperatures for stations where the species lives, drawn from its bell curve: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} with(filter(generative, present == "yes"), round(rnorm(5, mean, sd), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 7.5 6.1 9.2 6.7 9.1 ``` ::: ::: ## The two agree where the data are dense @fig-two-models puts the two side by side. The left panel is the generative model's view: the data of each group, and the bell curve it fitted. The right panel shows the answer both models give, the chance of presence at every temperature. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} curves <- tibble(temperature_c = seq(2, 16, by = 0.1)) |> mutate( Discriminative = predict(discriminative, pick(temperature_c), type = "prob")$.pred_yes, Generative = p_present_generative(temperature_c) ) |> pivot_longer(-temperature_c, names_to = "model", values_to = "p") bell <- generative |> reframe(temperature_c = seq(0, 18, by = 0.1), density = dnorm(temperature_c, mean, sd), .by = present) |> mutate(group = if_else(present == "yes", "Species found", "Species not found")) observed <- train |> mutate(band = round(temperature_c)) |> summarise(p = mean(present == "yes"), stations = n(), .by = band) |> filter(stations >= 10) p_data <- ggplot(mutate(train, group = if_else(present == "yes", "Species found", "Species not found")), aes(temperature_c, fill = group)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 1, alpha = 0.45, position = "identity", colour = NA) + geom_line(data = bell, aes(temperature_c, density, colour = group), linewidth = 1, inherit.aes = FALSE) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Density", fill = NULL, colour = NULL, title = "The generative model learns the data") p_chance <- ggplot(curves, aes(temperature_c, p, colour = model)) + geom_point(data = observed, aes(band, p), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey55", size = 2) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = unname(ml_palette[c("green", "purple")])) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Chance the species is present", colour = NULL, title = "Both give a chance of presence") p_data + p_chance ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: the generative view, the temperatures at stations with and without the species, each summarised by a bell curve. Right: the chance of presence against temperature from both models, with the observed proportion in each one-degree band as points. The two models agree where most stations lie and part company at the edges.](discriminative-and-generative-models_files/figure-html/fig-two-models-1.png){#fig-two-models fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel shows two histograms of temperature with a bell curve over each: stations with the species cluster between about 6 and 12 degrees, stations without it spread from about 3 to 15 degrees. The right panel shows two curves of the probability of presence against temperature, both rising from low values at 2 degrees to a peak near 0.85 to 0.9 around 9 degrees and falling again towards 16 degrees; the logistic curve falls more steeply at both ends. Points for the observed proportions follow the curves in the middle.' width=1700} ::: ::: | | Discriminative | Generative | | --- | --- | --- | | Learns | The chance of presence at each temperature | The temperatures in each group, and how common each group is | | Answers "present or absent?" | Directly | Through Bayes' rule | | Can generate new stations | No | Yes | | Relies on | The shape of the probability curve | The shape of each group's data | Where most stations lie, between about 6 and 12 °C, the two agree closely. At the edges they part company, and the three new stations show it: at 5 °C the generative model is the more hopeful of the two. There the generative answer rests on its bell curves, and the stations without the species are not really bell-shaped: they sit at both ends of the range, not around a single middle. The discriminative model never had to describe them, so the wrong shape costs it nothing. That is the usual trade. A generative model can do more, but it depends on its description of the data being right. A discriminative model makes fewer assumptions about the data, which is one reason it is the usual default. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - A discriminative model learns the answer: the chance of an outcome at each value of the inputs. - A generative model learns the data themselves, and can generate new examples. The tools that write text or draw pictures are generative models. - Both can answer the same question, and agree where the data are dense. - A generative model depends on its description of the data; where that description is wrong, so are its answers. ::: ## Try it yourself Replace temperature with depth in both presence models. Do the discriminative and generative curves still agree where most stations lie?
